lessons.title: The Arabic Alphabet — الحروف الهجائية
lessons.explanation: Arabic has 28 letters, all consonants. Vowels are represented by small marks (harakat) written above or below letters. Arabic is written right-to-left. Letters change shape depending on their position in the word.
lessons.tip: Each Arabic letter has four forms: isolated, initial, medial, and final. Most are connected to neighboring letters.

quiz.question: In which direction is Arabic written?
How many letters does the Arabic alphabet have?

lessons.title: Nouns — Gender and Definiteness
lessons.explanation: Arabic nouns are either masculine or feminine. Feminine nouns usually end in تاء مربوطة (ة). To make a noun definite (the), add ال (al-) at the beginning. The sun letters cause the 'l' to assimilate to the following letter.
lessons.tip: There is no indefinite article in Arabic (no word for 'a/an'). An unmodified noun is automatically indefinite.

quiz.question: How do you make an Arabic noun definite?
What ending usually marks a feminine Arabic noun?

lessons.title: Pronouns — الضمائر
lessons.explanation: Key Arabic pronouns: أنا (anā) = I, أنتَ (anta) = you (masc.), أنتِ (anti) = you (fem.), هو (huwa) = he, هي (hiya) = she, نحن (naḥnu) = we, أنتم (antum) = you (plural), هم (hum) = they.
lessons.tip: Arabic distinguishes gender in second and third person — you must use the right pronoun for male or female.

lessons.title: Nominal Sentences — الجملة الاسمية
lessons.explanation: Arabic has nominal sentences (subject + predicate) that have NO verb 'to be' in the present tense. The subject and predicate simply stand next to each other. Example: أنا طالب = I (am) a student — no word for 'am'.
lessons.tip: In present tense, Arabic omits the verb 'to be'. Just say subject + predicate. The verb كان (kāna) is used for past tense.

quiz.question: How do you say 'The book is big' in Arabic?

lessons.title: Verb Roots — الجذور الثلاثية
lessons.explanation: Arabic verbs are built from 3-letter roots. The same root generates many related words. For example, the root ك-ت-ب (k-t-b) relates to writing: كَتَبَ (kataba) = he wrote, كِتَاب (kitāb) = book, مَكْتَب (maktab) = office/desk, كَاتِب (kātib) = writer.
lessons.tip: Understanding the root system helps you guess the meaning of unfamiliar words and learn vocabulary faster.

quiz.question: What root is shared by كتاب (book) and كاتب (writer)?

lessons.title: Verb Conjugation — Past Tense
lessons.explanation: The Arabic past tense (الماضي) uses the 3rd person masculine singular as the base form. Add suffixes for other persons. Example with كَتَبَ (kataba = he wrote): كَتَبْتُ (I wrote), كَتَبْتَ (you wrote, masc.), كَتَبَ (he wrote), كَتَبَتْ (she wrote), كَتَبْنَا (we wrote).
examples: ذَهَبَ إلى المدرسة. (He went to school.)
lessons.tip: The past tense suffix -تُ marks 1st person singular (I). Past tense is the simplest tense to learn in Arabic.

quiz.question: What suffix marks 'I' in Arabic past tense?

lessons.title: Dual and Plural — المثنى والجمع
lessons.explanation: Arabic has three numbers: singular, dual (exactly two), and plural. Dual: add ان- (ān) to the noun. Plural is complex — there are sound plurals (add ون/ات) and broken plurals (internal vowel change, must be memorized). Example: كِتَاب → كِتَابَان (two books) → كُتُب (books, broken plural).
lessons.tip: Broken plurals must be memorized individually — there is no predictable pattern like in English.

quiz.question: How do you form the dual in Arabic?
